extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of Rabelais; and users/distributors of Project Gutenberg eBooks
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the literary qualities and textual/edition issues of Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel as presented in this Project Gutenberg edition, and understanding the licensing/redistribution obligations for the eBook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of contrasting tones
rubrics_metrics.description: The work is judged by its mixture of opposites: 'a mixture of mad mirth and gravity, of folly and reason, of childishness and grandeur, of the commonplace and the out-of-the-way, of popular verve and polished humanism, of mother-wit and learning, of baseness and nobility, of personalities and broad generalization, of the comic and the serious, of the impossible and the familiar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value is placed on the successful integration of these contrasts; the introduction emphasizes that this mixture is a defining and admirable quality of Rabelais' romance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality and intellectual force
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures the 'force of life and thought, such a power of good sense, a kind of assurance so authoritative' that mark great writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work that exhibits life, thought, good sense and authoritative assurance ranks highly; the introduction asserts these characteristics place Rabelais among the greatest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for both amusement and study
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful work both amuses and rewards repeated, deeper study: 'After being amused by it, after having enjoyed it, we may return again to study it and to enter more fully into its meaning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the text invites both immediate enjoyment and sustained scholarly engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and limits) of coarse/studied coarseness
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency toward 'occasional studied coarseness' is criticized as something that 'is enough to spoil his whole work, and which lowers its value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate whether ribaldry or coarse passages are gratuitous and harmful to the work's overall value, referencing La Bruyère's critical perspective given in the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/classical precedent for licentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptability of coarse or licentious material is to be judged in historical context: the Ancients (Aristophanes, Catullus, Petronius, Martial) and Renaissance Italian and English examples provided similar licence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating coarseness, consider whether Rabelais follows classical models and Renaissance conventions that legitimize playful or obscene elements in literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical provenance and textual editing
rubrics_metrics.description: The edition's textual decisions matter: note which printed editions/translations are used, which passages were restored or omitted, and the provenance of footnotes (e.g., 'The text of the first Two Books ... reprinted from the first edition (1653) of Urquhart's translation' and restorations from other editions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editions/translations by transparency about sources, editorial restorations, and annotations; transcriber's notes about editions and footnote attributions are important for scholarly use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical inference from textual references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use references within the work (names, persons, places) as evidence to infer authorial biography where external documentation is sparse: 'it is in the references in his romance to names, persons, and places, that the most certain and valuable evidence is to be found of his intercourse, his patrons, his friendships, his sojournings, and his travels.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing an author's life, give weight to internal textual evidence, but treat legends and anecdotes cautiously.
